activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
story:
Jacob wanted the good table, the one by the window with the kettle and the plate of samosas, and the problem was that Table One had already claimed it. The community centre's heritage night had split into four tables for the games, and the split had been done by Mr. Okafor pulling names out of a cereal bowl, which felt fair and turned out not to be.

By seven thirty, Table Two, Jacob's table, was chanting "Two, two, two" at Pictionary. Table Three had a secret handshake nobody could have learned in two hours, because two hours was all that had existed of Table Three. Table Four had started calling Table One "the window hogs." Jacob had been dumped into Table Two between Priya, who was telling everyone about her grandmother's Diwali lamps with meticulous, loving detail, and a kid named Marcus who claimed his family invented barbecue, which Jacob doubted but let slide.

"We've known each other since six o'clock," Jacob said to Priya. "Why are we cheering like we're a tribe?"

"Because we're Table Two," she said, as if that explained anything.

It bothered him the way a loose tooth bothers you. He had read something once, in his sister's psychology book, about a man named Tajfel who ran experiments where people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random. Jacob had skipped past it at the time. Now he watched Marcus guard the felt-tip pens from Table Three like they were family heirlooms, and thought: that's us. We're the experiment. So he tested it. He stood on a chair and announced that the tables were random, that Mr. Okafor had drawn every name out of a bowl, that Table Two was not destiny.

It did not help. "So what," Marcus said. "We're still the best random table." Table Two applauded him. Jacob climbed down, the embarrassment warm in his ears, and considered the possibility that knowing about a thing does not switch it off.

But Priya had gone quiet, and when the samosa plate came out, she carried two over to the kids at Table One and asked what was in their dishes, and they turned out to be things their grandmothers made, with stories attached, and Jacob followed her. Mr. Okafor wandered by and tried to incorporate the moment into a speech about community, and Jacob said, "We're just eating, sir." The window table had room after all. Marcus arrived last, plate out, and said, "This doesn't make us friends."
"We're not tables," said Priya. "We're just hungry people near a window."
Marcus bit into a samosa. "Okay," he said. "That one's mine."

story:
The trumpet wasn't working out, so Hailey switched to the flute, and now she had a new problem: reading music. She sat in the corner of the community center music room with a folded sheet of paper, glaring at the five lines and the fancy swirl at the start of every line. Her friend Marisol came over and dropped into the chair beside her.

"You look like the paper insulted you," Marisol said.

"I can find middle C. That's it. Then everything else is guessing." Hailey tapped the swirl. "And this thing just sits there like it's decoration."

Marisol leaned in. "My cousin plays piano. She calls that the G clef."

"The what?"

"G clef. That's the other name for it."

Hailey frowned at the symbol. A clef called G should mean something. She grabbed a pencil and copied the swirl onto her notebook, big and sloppy. Then she laid her flute sheet next to it and traced the curl slowly with her pencil tip, the way you'd trace a maze. The swirl looped around, dipped down, and curled back up, and where it curled it wrapped around the second line from the bottom. She checked her beginner book's note chart. The note on that line was G.

"No way," she whispered. The clef wasn't decoration. It was a marker, curling around the exact line where G lived, like a ring on a finger.

She tested it. G on the line, one space above was A, the line above that was B, and so on up the ladder. She played the little exercise from her book, and the notes came out in the right order for the first time. She played it again, faster, and grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

Marisol pointed at the door. "Little kids are coming for vaccine day. The nurse is setting up in the big room, so we have ten more minutes before they kick us out."

"Ten minutes is plenty," Hailey said. "It's not trivial to me. This was the whole wall in my way."

A small boy in a dinosaur shirt peeked into the music room while waiting for his shot, looking scared. Marisol waved him over. Hailey held up her notebook, showed him the swirl, and traced the curl around the second line. "See the loop? It's holding one spot so you never get lost." The boy forgot to be nervous long enough to trace it with his own finger.

When the nurse called his name, he walked out taller, and Marisol hurried after him with his jacket. Hailey packed up her flute, but she tore the notebook page out first and pressed it flat inside her book, the page she knew she would cherish on every practice day to come.

"Same time Thursday?" Marisol called from the doorway.

"Bring your cousin's number," Hailey said, tucking the flute under her arm. "I have questions."

story:
Lily sat cross-legged on Maya's bedroom floor with Maya's phone balanced on her knees, tapping through photos from Saturday. There was the one of Maya at the ice cream place, grinning with a double scoop. There was the one at the mall fountain. And there was the one Lily had taken of Maya outside Maya's own front door, because Maya had insisted the lighting was perfect.

"Send me the fountain one," Lily said, then stopped. "Wait. How many people can see these?"

"Just us. And my cousins. And probably the group chat." Maya flopped backward onto her pillow. "And that game I play, Frost Fox. It kind of posts stuff sometimes."

"Frost Fox posts your photos?"

"No, no. It posts where I am. Like, 'Maya unlocked the Glacier Zone at Maple Mall!' My aunt commented on it from two states away. She said, weren't you supposed to be at soccer?"

Lily scrolled to the game. A little map pin blinked beside a picture of a fox in a scarf, and next to the fox, Maya's last three locations were listed like trophies. Lily thought about the coyote that had wandered into their neighborhood last winter, how it had seemed to hibernate somewhere unseen all day and appear only at dusk, always knowing exactly which trash cans to visit. Someone had told her the coyote followed patterns, not luck. This felt like that, but backwards: the fox was following Maya.

"Can I check something?" Lily asked. She opened the phone's settings and hunted through screens until she found a list of apps with little arrows beside them. She recognized one arrow right away, because her dad had pointed at his own phone once and said, "That arrow means an app knows where you are." She tapped Frost Fox.

Three choices sat on the screen. Never. While using the app. Always.

"It's on Always," Lily said slowly. "That means it knew where you were even when you weren't playing."

Maya sat up so fast her ponytail whipped around. "You can pick?"

"You can pick for every app, one by one." Lily turned the phone so Maya could see. "My phone asks me the same thing. I always hit Always because I don't read the box. I just want the game to start."

"That's why Frost Fox knew I skipped soccer," Maya said, sounding both horrified and delighted. She jabbed the screen and switched the game to While Using. Then, defiant, she switched it to Never, just to watch the little map pin blink out.

Later, Lily texted her from home: did the fox die? Maya sent back a photo of Frost Fox wearing a blindfold, standing in an empty snowfield, with the caption "he asks where u at and I say none of ur business." Lily laughed out loud, then opened her own phone and went down her list of apps, one by one, arrow by arrow.

The last one, before bed, was a flashlight app. Always.

She stared at it. "You don't even know where I am," she told it, and pressed Never.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
story:
Alexis had spent every summer at Abuela's house since she was six, and every summer the streets had felt like a map she carried in her head. This summer Abuela had moved to a new neighborhood, and the map was gone. On the first morning, Abuela handed her a canvas bag. "Take these to the donation bin on Calle Rosa," she said. "And take the phone. In case."

Alexis did not take the phone. She had spent the school year failing Spanish, and she had decided the class was useless, so she left the phone on the table to prove she could manage without it. She walked three blocks carrying the bag of clothes she was meant to donate, and then the streets stopped matching anything Abuela had told her. A man was sweeping in front of a shop with green awnings. She stopped, and the dilemma was simple: ask in English and get nowhere, or try the Spanish she had decided she didn't have.

"¿Dónde está Calle Rosa?" she said.

The man answered fast, too fast, and then slowed down. "Sí. La primera calle a la izquierda." He pointed with his broom, but the street split ahead into two left turns, and she could not tell which one he meant. She knew izquierda meant left, that much had stuck. But which left came first?

She tried the other half of what her teacher had drilled into them, the part she'd thought she'd never use: repeat it back. "¿La primera calle a la izquierda?"

"Sí," the man said. "La primera." He held up one finger.

Alexis looked at the split. One left turn was really just a driveway into a parking area. The other was an actual street with a sign. If the driveway didn't count as a street, then the real street was the first one, the one with the sign. She said "Gracias," walked on, and watched. The driveway went into a lot full of cars. It was not a street. The sign at the second left said Rosa.

The bin stood at the corner, next to a bakery. She pushed the clothes in, and the bakery door swung open behind her. It was the man with the broom, holding a paper bag. "You found it," he said in English. "First street on the left."

"You speak English?" Alexis said.

"All my life." He shrugged. "Your grandmother asked me to keep an eye out. She said you'd refuse the phone." He held up the bag. "Come, she ordered bread. And she says I make the best empanadas in the city, but that is subjective."

Alexis laughed and followed him down Rosa. On Monday, she decided, she would ask Abuela to speak only Spanish at breakfast. She took out her phrase list on the walk home and read it twice.

The group chat lit up at 4:02 on a Saturday: "Dude, why are you at GameStop? I thought you were broke." Brayden stared at his phone. He had told nobody he was going to the mall. He had left the house saying he was "going for a walk," which was technically true if you counted walking to the bus. He typed back, "how do u know where I am," and Marcus answered with a screenshot of a map. There was a little cartoon face on it, standing right on top of the GameStop dot at the Westfield mall. Brayden looked at the ceiling of the store, then at the exit, as if the answer might be floating somewhere between them.

"Bro, that's the Snap Map," Marcus wrote. "It shows your real-time location to your friends on a map." Brayden read it twice. Real-time. He thought about all the times he'd wandered around after school, killing time before his mom got home, and how somebody could have been watching a little cartoon version of him do it the whole while. Weird feeling, like discovering his shoes had been narrating his day out loud.

He decided to test it. It seemed like an inevitable part of figuring things out; you couldn't just panic, you had to run an experiment. His technique was simple: he would walk from GameSpot to the pretzel stand two stores down, and if the cartoon face moved too, then the map was tracking him right now, not showing some old, harmless record. He bought a pretzel he didn't even want, mostly for cover, and stood under the big yellow sign eating it with the concentration of a scientist. Marcus sent a new screenshot. The face was on the pretzel stand. "Enjoy your pretzel," he wrote, adding three crying-laughing faces.

Brayden nearly choked. "This is so creepy," he typed with one thumb, pretzel in the other hand. But another thought itched at him, the curious kind. If it knew where he was, who else could see it? Marcus was his friend, sure. But the settings had layers, he'd heard people mention "friends of friends" like it was nothing. Somewhere out there, maybe strangers were watching the little cartoon face eat its little cartoon pretzel. He wondered how many eyes a dot could collect before the dot's owner even noticed.

Back home, he dug into the app's settings until he found the map options and switched his sharing to Ghost Mode. Then he typed into the group chat, "ok new rule, if anyone knows where I am, it's because I told them." Marcus replied with a single face, the one wearing sunglasses, and a message: "Meet me at the arcade in ten?"

Brayden grabbed his jacket. "Bring quarters," he wrote back, and hit send.

story:
Nora slid her vocabulary list across the desk and sighed. Fifteen word histories by Friday, and the definitions in the back of the book were so tedious that her eyes kept sliding off the page. The last word was "propaganda," and she almost skipped it, except that word had been bothering her all week. Marcus's posters for class president were everywhere, and something about them felt off, like a picture hung slightly crooked.

One poster said EVERYBODY'S CHOOSING MARCUS, with a long line of smiling kids drawn underneath it. Another called his opponent's ideas "dangerous" and "reckless," words that sounded exciting but meant nothing exactly. The biggest poster of all showed TJ, the eighth grader who could dunk, holding a thumbs-up: "TJ says Marcus is the real deal." Nora couldn't point to a single lie in any of them, and that was what made her uneasy. She flipped to the library's dictionary of word origins and ran her finger down the page.

There it was. The word came from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. Nora read the line twice, then copied it into her notebook. She raised her hand before she could talk herself out of it. "Mr. Reyes, I found where propaganda comes from. The Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622." A boy near the window snickered, and Nora felt her face go hot, but she kept going. "So it just meant spreading an idea around. It didn't start out as a bad word."

That night she tested a theory. If Marcus's posters worked by making people feel like everyone else had already decided, then a poster that pointed at the trick itself might break the spell. She made her own poster, plain and loud: "WHY DOES IT SAY EVERYBODY? ASK SOMEBODY." Underneath she drew a tiny panda chewing bamboo, with the caption "Pandas are herbivores. They eat facts, not hype." It was a strange joke, and she knew it, but she taped it up anyway, right between two of Marcus's.

By lunch, kids were standing in front of it. "What's a fact panda?" someone asked, and Nora said, "It only eats things that are actually true." Priya, who had been on the fence for a week, laughed and said, "Okay, that poster just got my vote for best poster. Marcus's are all sparkle and no sandwich." Marcus himself came down the hall, stopped, and read it twice. He peeled off his EVERYBODY'S CHOOSING MARCUS poster and looked at Nora over the top of it. "So what would a poster look like," he asked, "if I actually told people what I want to do?"

story:
The drive to the coast had taken six hours, and Ethan had spent most of it reading the state park brochure he found in the glove box. His sister Maya said he was biased because he'd already decided the beach would be better than their trip to the mountains last summer. "You only like it because you found that sand dollar," she said. Ethan put the brochure in his back pocket anyway.

That evening a ranger named Ms. Okafor gathered everyone at the fire ring behind the dunes for a talk about national parks. "Whoever answers the final question wins a junior ranger badge," she announced. "The question comes in ten minutes, at sunset, so talk it over now." Ethan's dad immediately claimed he knew everything about parks. Maya said the first one was probably Yosemite. Dad shook his head and said the Grand Canyon, since it was the biggest.

Ethan didn't shout out a guess. Instead he thought about what he'd read in the brochure while the waves hissed in the dark behind them. There had been a whole paragraph about Yellowstone, and he was almost sure he'd seen a date there, and a president's name. It felt like remembering where he'd left his shoes: he couldn't see the page, but he could picture sitting on it. He tested the memory by saying it out loud under his breath. "March 1, 1872. Grant." It sounded like something he'd actually read, not something he'd invented.

The sun touched the water and Ms. Okafor held up her hand. "Final question. Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when which president signed it into law?" Dad whispered "Roosevelt." Maya whispered "Lincoln." Ethan raised his hand so fast he knocked over his cup of cocoa.

"Ulysses S. Grant," he said. Ms. Okafor smiled and pinned the badge to his jacket. Dad threw his hands up. "I was going to say Grant," he said. "You were going to say Roosevelt," said Maya. "I was collecting my thoughts," said Dad, and everyone laughed, even Ethan.

Walking back to the cabin, Maya poked the badge. "Fine, the beach trip is better than the mountains. For now." Ethan crouched by the tideline, where a dead crab was slowly starting to decompose among the kelp, and picked up a spiral shell. "Trade you," he said, holding it out. "Badge for shell." Maya snatched it and ran up the dunes shouting, "No take-backs!"

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
story:
At dinner Tyler kept glancing at his older sister Priya, who was shoving noodles around her plate with a textbook propped against the milk carton. "Chapter five," she groaned. "There's this test from 1985, the Sally-Anne test, and there's a quiz on it tomorrow."

"Sally Anne is a doll," Priya said. "Sally puts her marble in a basket and leaves. While she's gone, someone moves the marble to a box. Then kids have to say where Sally will look for it." She tapped the page. "Kids from about age four usually say she'll look where she left it, the basket, not where it was moved. Little kids just can't believe Sally could be wrong about something."

Tyler looked down the table at their cousin Marcus, who was four and a half and busy building a tower out of sugar packets. "Wait," Tyler said. "You mean Marcus doesn't know that other people can be wrong?"

"He doesn't know that other people can believe something false," Priya said. "Nobody at this table believes the same thing about the meatloaf, and we all heard Mom's opinion on the school funding census at the last town meeting, so you know we're all capable of opposing each other politely." She grinned at Mom, who had spent two weeks arguing for a recount.

"Marcus," Tyler said, sliding a fork out of the drawer and hiding a sugar packet under it. "I'm putting my treasure under the fork. Watch." Marcus watched with enormous eyes. "Now I'm going to the kitchen. Don't touch it." Tyler walked out, stood against the refrigerator for ten seconds, and listened. When he came back, the fork was in exactly the same place, but Marcus's elbow was suspiciously close and one sugar packet was missing from the tower. Tyler knelt down. "Marcus. Where am I going to look for my treasure?"

Marcus pointed at the drawer. "You're gonna look in the drawer, 'cause you didn't see."

Tyler sat back on his heels. He'd been sure Marcus would point at the fork, because that's where Tyler had put the treasure, and that's what mattered, right? But Marcus had tracked the whole thing: Tyler left, Tyler didn't see the move, so Tyler's mind still held the old picture. Four and a half years old, and he already knew that what you saw wasn't the same as what somebody else knew. Priya was the one who'd gotten it wrong, at least about Marcus.

"Priya," Tyler called. "Wrong kid. He passed." He turned back to Marcus, took the fork, and lifted it slowly. The sugar packet was gone from underneath, and in its place sat a folded napkin with "SORRY" written in wobbling crayon letters.

"You can have this instead," Marcus said, holding out the sugar packet with both hands. "I only borrowed it."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out while Alicia was watering her grandmother's tomato plants, and the porch swallowed itself into darkness so fast it felt like the evening had decided to accelerate. She stood in the backyard holding the dripping can, listening. No hum from the air conditioner. No glow from the kitchen window.

"Grandma?" she called, and heard shuffling inside. Her grandmother found her at the back door with a flashlight, its beam small and unimpressive next to the extravagant chandelier that hung, useless and dark, in the hallway. Grandma's cordless phone sat in its cradle on the counter, and when she picked it up and pressed talk, nothing happened. Not even static.

"Battery must be dead," Grandma said, tapping it against her palm.

Alicia took the phone and turned it over. "It's plugged into the wall," she said slowly. "The base is, anyway. If the power's out, maybe the phone isn't dead. Maybe the outlet is." Grandma raised an eyebrow, which was her way of saying go on. Alicia set the handset down and stood still, thinking. The phone needed the house's electricity. That part made sense. But something nagged at her, an old memory of phones with curly cords and no plugs at all. How had those ever worked? It seemed like a paradox, a thing with no power cord that still had power. Unless the power came from somewhere else.

"Grandma, did you ever have one of those wall phones? The kind with the cord?"

"Kitchen. Still there, behind the biscuit tin. I keep it because I hate throwing away anything that works."

Alicia pushed the tin aside and found it, a heavy cream-colored phone bolted to the wall with a cord coiled like a spring. No plug, no battery compartment. She lifted the receiver and held it to her ear, half expecting silence. Instead, a dial tone buzzed, steady and alive, as if the power cut had never happened. She nearly dropped it.

"Grandma! It works!" she shouted. "The line gets its power from the phone company, not from our house. That's why it still works."

"Well, I'll be," Grandma said, and then, because she was Grandma, "Call your mother before she worries."

Alicia dialed, and when her mother answered on the first ring, breathless and already reaching for her car keys, Alicia had to talk fast to keep her from driving over in the dark. "We're fine. We have flashlights, the stove is gas, and I found a phone that doesn't need electricity at all." Outside, a neighbor's generator roared to life, and somewhere down the block a dog barked at it. Alicia sat on the kitchen floor, the coiled cord stretching to reach her, and told her mother about the tomato plants she'd been watering when the world went dark. The dial tone hummed softly under her voice the whole time.

story:
Gabriel had babysat exactly nobody before Saturday, which was why Mrs. Yi leaving him alone with eight-month-old Penny felt like being handed a live grenade and a smile. The instructions on the fridge ran to two pages, front and back, in handwriting so small he had to lean in until his nose nearly touched the paper. Behind him, from the playpen, Penny made a sound like a small, judgmental owl.

Everything went fine for an hour. Penny ate her cereal, gravity took its usual cut, and Gabriel learned that a baby could inhale a fistful of banana faster than he would have believed possible. Then Penny stopped eating. She pressed her lips together and turned her face away from the spoon with the determination of a soccer goalie defending a net. Gabriel tried the airplane trick, the choo-choo trick, and the desperate humming trick. Nothing. He looked at the cereal, which was plain oat mush, and thought the problem was obvious: it was boring. He got the honey jar from the pantry and had the lid half off when he noticed a line at the bottom of page two, underlined twice.

No honey, it said. Not until she's over 12 months. Bacteria spores in it can grow in her gut. That last word had sent Mrs. Yi's pen skidding. Gabriel stood there with the jar, rereading it. He'd never once thought of honey as something that could hide trouble. It just sat there looking golden and harmless, like a trap designed by someone with a grudge against toast. He put the lid back on and returned it to the pantry, feeling the embarrassment arrive about one second too late to stop him from having opened it in the first place.

Penny still refused the cereal, so Gabriel got systematic. If the problem wasn't taste, maybe it was temperature. He touched the bowl: cold. The instructions said warm it for twenty seconds, and he'd been so busy with airplanes he'd skipped that step. He tested the idea, microwaved the bowl, stirred it, and offered the spoon again. Penny considered him with the flat stare of an emperor, then opened her mouth like a garage door. The entire bowl vanished in four minutes.

Mrs. Yi came home to find the kitchen clean, the honey jar in its exact spot in the pantry, though it was turned two degrees from where it had been, and Penny asleep in the playpen. "How was she?" she asked.

"Fine," Gabriel said. "Great, actually." He did not mention the honey, or page two, or the fact that his heart had gone briefly extinct in his chest when he'd read it. He took his twenty dollars, and at the door he paused. "Next time could you underline that honey part at the top? Maybe in red."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
story:
Tristan discovered the problem at seven o'clock on Tuesday morning, in the driveway, with the car still cold. He had been singing along with the radio, loudly, the way nobody could hear him, when the word "tonight" came out in two pieces. The "to" was high and normal, and the "night" dropped straight down into some gravelly cave he had never visited before. He tried it again. "Tonight." It cracked again, right in the middle, like a stick snapping.

In the car on the way to school, his sister Maya noticed him experimenting. "Why do you keep saying 'ahhh' like a dying robot?" she asked, buckling her seatbelt. Tristan ignored her, which was not easy, because the car was small and Maya was never indifferent to a chance to tease him. He was busy. He hummed a low note, then a high one, then the note in between where the break lived. It was like there were two voices inside him, an old one and a new one, and no bridge between them yet.

By Thursday he had begun to classify the evidence. Low notes worked fine. Talking worked fine, mostly. High notes were the problem, and the break always happened in the same narrow spot. Dad drove them to choir practice that evening, and Tristan spent the whole ride testing his newest idea: if he sang quietly enough, maybe the crack couldn't get enough air to happen. He whispered scales in the back seat. Maya put in her earbuds. "It still cracks," Tristan reported, half thrilled, half annoyed. "Just quieter."

At practice, Marcus got the solo in the new song, and Marcus sailed through the verse and then hit the big high note at the end, and his voice split exactly the way Tristan's had. Mr. Ruiz raised one hand. "Marcus's larynx is growing," he said, "so the vocal folds inside it are getting longer and thicker, and they may crack while that happens." Marcus turned red, but Tristan nearly fell off the riser. Folds. Longer and thicker. That was it. That was the hidden machine.

On the drive home, Tristan leaned forward between the front seats. "Dad, the vocal folds get longer and thicker, and that's why the voice drops. It's like a guitar string, kind of. Except inside." Dad glanced at him in the mirror. "A metaphor," Dad said. "Sure. Every guy in this car went through it." Maya pulled out one earbud. "Even Dad cracked?" "Ask your grandmother," Dad said. "I once scared the dog."

Tristan sat back. The car hummed along the dark road, and he hummed with it, low, in the new voice, the one with no cracks in it at all. He was already planning the choir solo for next year. "Marcus," he said to the window, "your solo is mine in October."

story:
Georgia had measured her bean plants twice, and both times the numbers made her stomach drop. The six pots on the windowsill, the ones she had watered every morning with the special fertilizer her grandmother sent, had grown three inches in two weeks. That was the good part. The bad part was the question her friend Priya had asked at lunch: "Grown three inches compared to what?"

Now, in the kitchen, Georgia laid her science notebook on the counter and stared at her chart. Six plants, all fertilized, all tall. Beside the sink her little brother Theo was gluing popsicle sticks into what he claimed was an authentic Viking longship, though it looked more like a raft with ambitions. "You keep frowning at that notebook," he said. "Is it going to bite you?"

"Priya says my project doesn't prove anything. Maybe the beans would have grown three inches anyway." Georgia tapped her pencil against the page. Her instinct told her the fertilizer worked, but instinct wasn't allowed in the results section. "If I can't compare them to something, I can't tell."

Theo set down his glue. "Compare them to what, the Viking ship?"

The pharmacy smelled like soap and cough drops, and Kate stood by the shelf of shoe inserts while her mother picked up a prescription. In the basket under her arm sat a box of plasters, a comb, and the money she had saved for the display rack behind the counter. Kate turned the idea over while her mother talked to the pharmacist about antihistamines. Her premise was simple: if Tom's feet were growing, the rest of him should be growing too, at the same time. That was how she had always assumed growing worked, everything at once, like inflating a balloon. But the evidence did not fit. Ruth laughed. "No. Hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms and legs and the rest of the body catch up."

"So the legs will catch up," Kate said. "Later."

"That's the usual order," Ruth said, and rang up a packet of plasters for the woman behind them.

Kate stood there doing the sums. Tom looked at her, then at his feet. "How do you know?"

Kate tapped his shoe with her own. "Your feet told me."

Penelope tapped her pencil against the gym door and counted the seconds until Coach Ruiz stopped talking. He was explaining the wall chart again, the one with every girl's free-throw percentage ranked from best to worst, and Penelope's name was near the bottom. Again. She shot every day at the park, sometimes fifty times, and her ranking never moved. Something was wrong with the chart, or something was wrong with her, and she intended to find out which.

That Saturday, her uncle Marcelo took her to Riley's, the sports bar near his apartment, because her parents were at a conference and somebody had to supervise her while they were gone. Uncle Marcelo wanted the place mostly for the nachos, which he claimed were the best in the county, and he wanted them extra hot. On the big screen, two baseball announcers were arguing about a player. One of them kept saying "on-base percentage" like it was a magic spell.

"That guy's boring," the other announcer said. "Everyone knows home runs win games."

Uncle Marcelo laughed through a mouthful of chips. "There's a book about this. Came out in 2003, written by Michael Lewis. It's called Moneyball. The 2002 Oakland Athletics, the whole team, they didn't have money like the rich teams. So they used statistics like on-base percentage to find players nobody else wanted. Cheap players. Undervalued, that's the word. And they competed anyway."

"You mean the team with the least money won?" Penelope asked.

"Competed," her uncle said, holding up a nacho like a professor's chalk. "That's the important part." Then he ordered a second plate and forgot the whole conversation, but Penelope didn't.

Monday after school, she sat in the library with the chart numbers she had copied into her notebook and a library copy of the book itself, which was thicker than she expected and, she discovered by page thirty, kind of tedious in places. The idea underneath it wasn't tedious at all. Home runs and total points and rankings were just the loud numbers. There were quieter numbers that told you what a player actually did over and over, game after game.

She found a table where her friend Dree was drawing a poster for the pet club, some cartoon herbivore munching leaves. "Dree," Penelope said, "you know the book report you did on dolphins? Where'd you get the database?"

"Library site. Why?"

Penelope borrowed the computer and typed in the coach's practice log, which was posted online every week. She felt like she was doing something slightly against the rules, even though it wasn't. The log had everyone's attempts and makes for three whole weeks. The chart on the gym wall only showed one number per player, and Penelope's number looked bad because she took the most attempts of anyone on the team. Sixty-one attempts. The captain, Roni, had taken twelve and made nine, which put her first on the chart.

Penelope did the division four times to be sure. Over the three weeks, Penelope's percentage was higher than Roni's. Not by much. But higher.

The next morning she asked Coach Ruiz if she could show him something, and she laid her notebook on his desk next to his coffee. He frowned at it for a long moment, the way he frowned at blown plays. "Where'd you get this?"

"The practice log. And a book." She pointed at the column of divisions. "The chart squishes everything into one number."

Coach Ruiz rubbed his jaw. Then he stood, walked to the gym wall, and drew a second column in green marker next to the old one. "Practice attempts logged, three-week average," he announced to the arriving team, and the room went quiet the way it did before a close game's final shot.

Roni stared at the new column, at her name, and then at Penelope's name sitting two lines above it. "How long have you been shooting sixty a day?"

"Since October," Penelope said.

Roni picked up a ball from the rack and bounced it once, hard. "Fine. Then race me to a hundred makes."

story:
The festival filled the park with tents and flags, and Edouard moved through the crowd with a folded card in his back pocket. His grandmother had pressed it into his hand that morning before he left, saying in their family's language, "This is for you, but read it at the lantern table, not before." Edouard understood every word she said. He had been answering her in that language since he was small, at Sunday dinners and on the phone every Thursday. But the card itself was written down, in looping script he could not read at all.

He found the lantern table near the fountain, where volunteers were handing out translucent paper shades for people to decorate and hang on the long strings overhead. Painting a message on a lantern before hanging it was the closing ritual of the festival, and his grandmother had done it every year since they arrived. Edouard unfolded the card, hoping that seeing the whole thing would somehow help. It didn't. The letters sat there like a fence he could walk beside but never get through. He spoke the language, and yet the writing was a stranger to him.

At the next table, a girl about his age was chatting easily with an elderly woman in a language Edouard recognized as the same one. Then the woman handed her a small note, and the girl's face went pink. "Halmoni, I can't read this," she admitted. "I can talk to you fine, but reading it is different." The older woman laughed kindly and read it aloud herself. Edouard drifted closer. "Same thing happens to me," he said. "I chat with my grandmother all the time, but I can't read a word she writes."

The girl, whose name was Naomi, nodded like she'd been waiting for someone to say it. "My cousin calls ours a heritage language," she said. "Because we speak it at home, but out here everyone uses the community's main language." She tapped the note. "So kids like us can speak it and still not read it." Edouard looked back at his card. It wasn't that he was bad at the language. It was that speaking it and reading it were two different skills, and only one of them had ever been needed at his house.

He had an idea. If the grandmother could read the note aloud, maybe he could test whether his ear could do the work his eyes couldn't. He asked Naomi's grandmother, politely, if she would read his card to him. She unfolded it, smiled at the looping script, and spoke the words slowly. As she read, Edouard followed along, and the sentence opened like a door: "Write your wish for the year on your lantern, in our language, any way you can."

His grandmother hadn't asked for perfect spelling. She'd only asked him to try. Edouard picked up a brush, dipped it in the deep blue paint, and, letter by careful letter, copying from the card in front of him, began to write.

In thirty minutes the regional spelling bee would start, and only the champion would go to nationals. Second place got a dictionary, which felt to Grace like getting a towel after swimming halfway across a pool. Across the aisle, Marcus leaned his head against the window and watched the fence posts go by.

"You look like you're going to be sick," Grace said.

"I might be," Marcus said. "If I come in second again. Last year I got out on 'rhubarb.' Do you know how it feels to lose to a vegetable?"

Grace opened her mouth to say she didn't care about his rhubarb, then closed it, because the truth was she had thought about little else all week except coming in second herself. She reached into her backpack and pulled out a folded note her older sister had left on her pillow that morning. She smoothed it out on her knee.

"If you get 'presume' in the bee, it's p-r-e-s-u-m-e," her sister had written, "because you presume you're right before you check. Don't presume. Ask for the definition every single time. She spelled "anomaly," asking for the definition first, exactly as the note said, and got it right. Round after round followed, and nobody missed. The pronouncer kept pulling fresh words from the box, and Grace noticed something she had never seen before: there was no rule for ending this. She remembered a fact her sister had mentioned once, and she raised her hand.

"Is it true that the 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right?"

The pronouncer blinked. "That's correct."

"So if we both keep spelling everything right," Grace said, "there doesn't have to be a loser?"

The officials conferred in the corner, and Marcus caught Grace's eye across the microphone. He was grinning now, not green at all. Two rounds later, after Grace sailed through "moratorium" and Marcus handled "vitreous" without a stumble, the pronouncer lifted his hand.

"We are declaring two co-champions," he announced. "Both of you will advance to nationals."

Marcus held up his fist across the stage, and Grace ran over and bumped it with hers. In the back of the hall, her sister was already on her feet, waving the empty note envelope over her head like a flag.

story:
Hannah crouched beside the boardwalk on the Willow Creek trail, her notebook open to a page titled "BIRD EVIDENCE" in fat letters. Her mission for the morning was to watch one bird for ten whole minutes and record what its beak did. Her little brother Marcus wanted only one thing: to reach the frog pond before anyone else in the history of the world. "Slow bird-watchers restrict the pace of fast civilians," he announced, drumming his heels on the boards.

"Shh. I think it's a wren," Hannah whispered, pointing at a stubby gray bird prying something out of a seed head. She drew the beak, small and curved like a bent nail. Then she checked her field guide, and her stomach dropped. The bird on the page had a straight, thick, seed-cracking beak. Her "wren" was a finch, and her whole page of careful notes now belonged to the wrong bird. She flopped back against the railing. "This is hopeless. Even Darwin's birds got mixed up, and I can't even tell a finch from a wren."

Marcus stopped drumming. "Darwin messed up birds? The Darwin?" He sat down, suddenly very interested in the idea of a famous genius being wrong.

Hannah flipped to the back of the guide, where a timeline ran along the bottom of the page. She ran her finger along it and stopped. "Listen to this. In 1837, an ornithologist named John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, some of which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were a new group of closely related finches." She read it twice, and something clicked into place. "So Darwin collected them and labeled them wrong. Gould looked at the beaks and saw what Darwin missed."

"Who's John Gould?" Marcus asked.

"Bird scientist. The one who figured it out." Hannah turned back to her notebook. On the Galápagos islands, she remembered from class, the finches on different islands had different beak shapes, each one matched to a different food. The beaks themselves were the evidence, sitting right there on the birds' faces. If a beak was thick, it cracked hard seeds. If it was thin, it grabbed insects. Nobody could watch the beaks changing over generations, but you could read the pattern, like footprints left by something you never saw. Maybe, she thought, mislabeling one bird wasn't a disaster. Maybe it was step one.

She crossed out "wren," wrote "FINCH," and drew the beak again, thicker this time, with an arrow pointing to it and the word "fundamental clue" beside it. "Your turn," she said, handing Marcus her pencil. "Draw the frog's mouth. Big or small? Wide or narrow? It matters, I promise."

Marcus took the pencil, raced down the boardwalk toward the pond, and skidded to a stop with his nose an inch from the water. "Huge," he reported. "It's a mouth finch."

Jake's fingers slid off the strings for the eleventh time, and the note came out sour, like a door complaining on its hinges. His grandfather's old guitar had a warm, honey-colored body that smelled faintly of lemon polish, and Jake loved everything about it except the fact that he couldn't play it. He had been at Grandpa's house every Saturday for a month, working through the same song from start to finish, over and over, and measure seventeen still collapsed every single time.

He set the guitar down and wandered into the kitchen, where Grandpa was folding a frugal lunch of half a sandwich and the last three crackers in the box. "Can I confide something?" Jake asked. "That song hates me."

"Songs don't hate people," Grandpa said, sliding the plate toward him. "But something in it might not like your fingers."

Jake chewed the cracker and thought about that. What exactly was going wrong? He hummed the piece in his head and noticed something odd. The beginning was smooth now. The ending, the big climax with all those ringing chords, was almost easy. Only four measures in the middle, the quick jump from the third string to the first, kept snapping like a trap. So why was he practicing the whole song, start to finish, when the whole song wasn't the problem?

He carried the guitar back to the porch rocker and tried a different idea. He would play only measures seventeen through twenty. Nothing else. He looped them slowly, slower than the song actually went, watching his fingers make the jump, missing, backing up, trying again. Then a little faster. Then faster still. Was this how real players did it? He wondered whether hours of playing a piece mattered less than aiming straight at the weak spot, like fixing the one broken stair instead of walking the whole staircase a hundred times.

After forty minutes his left hand ached and his fingertips had grooves in them, but the jump was starting to feel automatic, almost like blinking. He played the whole song once, and when measure seventeen arrived, his fingers simply knew where to go. He laughed out loud at the empty porch.

"That sounded different," Grandpa said from the doorway, holding two glasses of lemonade. "You fixed it."

"I fixed four measures," Jake said. "Just those."

Grandpa grinned. "Then tomorrow we'll find out what happens when you aim at the next four."

story:
Layla had claimed the scruffy plot at the far corner of the community garden because nobody else wanted it, and now she knew why. Every morning her seedlings leaned sideways like they were trying to escape. Her beans flopped over in a tangle. Her squash sat there looking depressed. Meanwhile, Mrs. Okafor's plot next door was so vigorous it practically hummed.

"Your beans need something to climb," Mrs. Okafor said, snapping a pea pod. "Come look at my plan."

Taped inside Mrs. Okafor's shed door was a hand-drawn map with circles inside circles. Corn in the center, beans around it, squash around everything. At the top, in curly letters, it said Three Sisters.

"That's what it's called," Mrs. Okafor said. "My grandmother planted it this way." She tapped the map with a soil-crusted finger. "Corn supports the climbing beans, and the squash leaves shade the soil against weeds."

Layla squinted at it. The corn was a fence post you could eat. The beans were the climbers. The squash was, what, a living mulch? She couldn't see any of that happening underground, or in the future, which was the problem with gardens. You had to bet on a pattern you couldn't watch.

So she tested it. She planted her remaining corn seeds in a tight cluster in the middle of her plot, bean seeds in a ring around them, and squash seeds along the outer edge. Her little brother Dev helped by naming every squash. "This one's Gary," he announced. "Gary is going to be enormous."

For two weeks nothing proved anything. Then, in July, the corn shot up, and the beans did exactly what Mrs. Okafor's map had promised. They wrapped around the cornstalks and climbed, one curl at a time, using the corn like a ladder. When a storm rolled through and cracked a branch off the mulberry tree, the corn bent but held. Not one bean pole, because there were no poles. The beans just held on tighter.

But the squash worried her. Three of them wilted, and she couldn't figure out why until she got a letter from Mrs. Okafor, who had gone to visit her sister in Ohio. It read: "Layla, water deep, not often. Squash roots fracture easy if you yank weeds beside them, so mulch instead. Your corn is taller than mine. I am pretending I am not jealous."

Layla watered deep and mulched around Gary and his friends, spreading straw with Dev, who insisted on tucking it in like blankets. By August the whole plot was a jungle. The squash leaves had spread so wide that the shaded ground underneath was bare, while weeds sprouted happily everywhere else. Dev pulled one weed, purely to prove it existed.

At the harvest dinner, Layla served corn, beans, and roasted Gary. Mrs. Okafor took seconds of everything.

"Admit it," Layla said. "Mine's better."

Mrs. Okafor chewed slowly. "I'll admit Gary," she said, and reached for a third helping.

The sign outside Dell's Gas and Go had slushies for a dollar, and Lucy wanted one so badly she could already feel the brain freeze. Her little brother Marcus wanted one too, plus a bag of chips, plus a lottery scratcher he was not going to get. But between them they had exactly one dollar and forty cents, and Lucy's dollar was spoken for.

"Look at that line," Marcus said. Seven people were crowded at the slushie machine, and the sound of the motor grinding ice filled the whole store. The kid ahead of Lucy, Devon from her science class, filled his cup to the very brim, then filled a second cup for his mom.

When Lucy finally got her turn, the machine sputtered and went quiet. Dell came out from behind the register, tapped the tank, and shook his head. "Machine's out of syrup till my delivery Friday. That's the last of it."

"Great," Lucy said. "So no slushie at all."

Dell shrugged. "Unless somebody wants to pay for what's left in the cup tray. I'm charging three dollars a cup now."

Marcus gasped like she'd asked him to hand over a kidney. "Three dollars? That's robbery!"

But Lucy was watching, not listening to Marcus. Of the seven people in line, only Devon and one trucker actually paid three dollars. The other five put their cups back and drifted toward the soda cooler, grumbling. Lucy chewed her lip. Fewer buyers, higher price. She'd seen the flip side that morning at the farmers market, when the peach lady dropped her price at closing time and got mobbed.

"Hey, Devon," she said. "In social studies, isn't there a name for that? When the price goes up and people buy less?"

"The law of demand," Devon said. "When prices rise, people buy less. When they drop, people buy more."

"That's it." Lucy turned to Dell. "What if you tried one dollar a cup instead? I bet more people would buy what's left, and you'd clear it out before Friday."

"I don't need a jury of thirteen-year-olds running my store," Dell said, but he was rubbing his chin, and the stack of unsold cups wasn't getting smaller on its own. "One hour. Dollar a cup. If it works, you get the first one free."

It worked. Lucy stood by the door and counted, because she wanted her numbers to be consistent before she claimed anything. In forty minutes the tray was empty, and a man in a lawn-mower company truck bought the very last two cups at once. The one thing Lucy couldn't see, the invisible rule underneath the buying and the selling, had behaved exactly the way she predicted, and that felt better than the slushie.

Dell handed her a free cup, cherry red. Marcus held out his hand, eyes enormous.

"You were going to intervene on my behalf, right?" he said. "Because I'm your brother? Because family?"

Lucy sucked down a long, cold sip, considered him over the rim of the cup, and handed him exactly one third.

"So they need a grown-up to say yes?"

"Or get Mom to sign." In the lobby behind them, DragonGrl99 was typing in all capitals again. Emilia muted it.

Maelie pressed her ear against the metal trash can in her grandfather's garage workshop and tapped the side with a screwdriver. A dull thud answered her, nothing more. For three nights the strange scratching had come from somewhere in the garage, and every morning the traps she set stayed empty.

"You're going to catch it eventually," her cousin Theo said from the workbench, where he was lettering her science fair board in thick blue marker. He had steady hands, and she envied him that, because her own letters always slid downhill. The board needed a section labeled "Hypothesis" and she had asked him to leave space for it.

"Not eventually," Maelie said. "Tonight. I think I know what it is." She stood back and looked at the garage the way her grandfather had taught her, watching for the paths things took. The scratching happened only after dark, always near the back wall, always above the shelf where he kept his old maps of the river estuary, those curling charts of where the current met the sea. Nothing that scratched could be seen by day, so it had to be something hidden, something with a reason for coming out only at night. Her guess was that a mouse had found the bag of birdseed on the top shelf, but guesses were not enough for a science fair.

She looked up "hypothesis" in the dictionary on the workbench and frowned at what she found. "It comes from ancient Greek," she read slowly, "and it literally means 'putting or placing under.'"

"Under what?" Theo asked.

"That's all it says. Putting or placing under." She copied it onto an index card. A hypothesis, she decided, was like the board's foundation, the guess you placed under everything else, and the experiment stood on top of it. If the experiment collapsed, you had guessed wrong.

That evening she set two traps. One went beside the birdseed on the top shelf, where her mouse idea said it belonged. The other went under the trash can, in case the sound was traveling along the wall from somewhere lower and fooling her ears. Sound could do that, bounce and mislead. In the morning she found the top trap sprung, a seed hull beside it, and a gray whiskered shape gone, but the trail of hulls led up behind the maps and through a gap into the ceiling. Her guess had been placed in the right spot after all, and it had held.

At the fair, the judge paused at her board. "So your hypothesis was supported," she said.

Maelie touched the index card glued beneath the title. "It means putting or placing under," she said. "The Greek. I looked it up." She thought of her grandfather, who had wanted her to keep the workshop, and how she had almost said no; that choice still sat with her, not fully settled. The judge smiled and moved on, and Maelie straightened the card so it sat exactly under the words above it.

The guest bedroom was the coldest room in the house, and Hazel knew it before she even opened the door. The floorboards chilled her bare feet, and the air smelled like dust and old lavender sachets from the closet. Her grandmother would sleep here for a whole week, starting tonight, and Hazel wanted everything to be perfect.

"You can have my quilt too," Hazel said, dragging the heavy blue bundle down the hall. "It's the warmest thing we own."

"That's kind of you, sweetheart." Grandma set her suitcase on the bed, moving with her usual careful steps. On the first night, Hazel checked on her before bed and found her tucked under both quilts, hands wrapped around a teacup she'd brought upstairs herself, her fingertips pale as paper. Grandma smiled and said the room was lovely. The radiator under the window was barely warm when Hazel pressed her palm against it.

She couldn't stop thinking about it the next morning. She remembered a school trip to the butterfly house two years ago, when the guide had explained that bees pollinate flowers by carrying pollen on their fuzzy legs, and how a small thing doing quiet work could keep something alive without anyone noticing. Her grandmother's cold hands felt like that, a small quiet signal of something bigger. So Hazel typed her question into the library computer, half sure she was being dramatic, and found what she needed in a paragraph she read three times: older adults face a greater risk of hypothermia than younger adults, a dangerous drop in body temperature, and they can get it even in a house that doesn't seem that cold, because they may not complain.

That afternoon she found her father arguing with her uncle on the phone about whether to replace the old furnace, a family controversy that had raged since Thanksgiving. Hazel waited until her father hung up, then showed him the paragraph on her screen.

"Hypothermia," she said. "That's what it's called. Grandma's room is freezing and she keeps saying it's fine."

Her father pressed his hand to the guest room radiator, the way Hazel had, and frowned. "You noticed something I missed," he said. "Let's fix it."

They carried up the space heater from the basement, and Hazel, who was small and agile, squeezed behind the dresser to plug it in where nobody else could reach. When Grandma came up after dinner, the room was toasty, and the smell of lavender had softened into something almost like a garden in July. Hazel watched her grandmother pull off the second quilt and settle in with just the sheet, her fingers pink again as she turned the pages of her novel.

"There was a drafty farm house where I raised your mother," Grandma said, patting the bed beside her. "I survived it, but I'm not sorry to skip that part this time." Hazel kicked off her slippers and climbed up next to her, tucking her cold toes under the warm edge of the blue quilt.

Adam had one job at the farmers' market: buy a jar of Mr. Ruiz's wildflower honey before it sold out. His grandmother's birthday was Saturday, and she'd said last month that his honey was the only thing she wanted. The problem was that everyone else's grandmother seemed to want it too, because Mr. Ruiz charged four dollars a jar when the other honey sellers charged nine.

By the time Adam reached the stall, the line stretched past the bread stand and curved around the corner. A woman near the front turned around and called back, "He's down to his last crate!" A groan rolled down the line like a wave. Adam stood on a crate to coordinate with his friend Priya, who was saving spots for each other whenever one of them needed to dash off, and waved to show her where he was. She held up two fingers. Twenty minutes from the front, maybe.

When Adam finally got there, a handwritten sign leaned against the empty crate: SOLD OUT, BACK NEXT WEEK. Next week was after the birthday. He stared at the sign, then at Mr. Ruiz, who was apologizing to person after person behind Adam. "Four dollars is my price," the man kept saying, shrugging. "I sell out by nine every week, and I hate turning folks away, but that's just what happens when more people want it than I've got." Adam walked back along the line, and it hit him: every single person still waiting wanted honey at four dollars. If it cost nine, like at the stall next door, half of them would probably walk away, and there would still be jars left. The gap between the crowd and the crates was the whole story.

"It's called a shortage," Priya said when he told her, still holding her tote bag. "My sister tried to get concert tickets last month. Cheap ones gone in four minutes, and hundreds of fans got nothing. She said that's the word for it, when the price is kept low and more people want the thing than there are things to sell." Adam looked back at Mr. Ruiz's empty crates, feeling the shape of the idea settle into place.

At the next stall, though, a farmer was practically hiding behind towers of zucchini. "Take a bag, take two," she told Adam, dropping the price from two dollars to one, then to fifty cents. Nobody wanted zucchini in August, not this much of it. Priya bought three and didn't even like zucchini. Adam bought a bag too, feeling a small flush of embarrassment for Mr. Ruiz and his stubborn four dollars, but also a plan forming.

"Could you do a trade?" he asked the woman. "My neighbor will trade you zucchini bread for honey. She does it every fall." The farmer thought, then nodded slowly. "Tell her to bring the bread Sunday. I've got jars." Adam texted his neighbor from the corner of the market, and she sent back a thumbs-up and three exclamation points. He walked home carrying zucchini for his grandmother's birthday bread, honey already promised, and Mr. Ruiz's empty crates still in his mind, waiting for next week.

Piper arrived at Mr. Alvarez's studio ten minutes early, holding her grandmother's old guitar by the neck. She had a note folded in her pocket, a message her grandmother had written before her hands got too stiff to play: "The twelfth fret holds a secret. Find it yourself." Piper had read it four times on the bus, and she presumed there was a real answer waiting, not just something her grandmother had made up to keep her practicing.

She tuned the low E string and plucked it once. The open string rumbled through the small room. Then she pressed her finger down at the twelfth fret, the one marked by two diagonal inlaid dots, and plucked again. A note came out that was clearly the same and not the same at all. It rang higher, and it matched something she recognized.

"You found it already," Mr. Alvarez said from his chair by the window. He was sorting sheet music and had not touched her guitar once.

"It's the same note," Piper said. "Only higher. A lot higher." She slid her finger along the string, checking. "The twelfth fret sits right in the middle of the string, doesn't it?"

"Measure it if you want," he said.

She borrowed a ruler from the desk drawer. The distance from the nut to the bridge was sixty-four centimeters. The twelfth fret sat at thirty-two, exactly halfway. She played the open string, then the fretted one, back and forth, listening. Pressing the string at its exact midpoint halved the length that could vibrate, and the note rose by a full octave. She tested the A string next, then the D, and it worked every time.

"I kept messing up at the seventh fret last week and I was starting to feel resentment toward this whole guitar," she said. "But this makes sense. It's not random."

Mr. Alvarez smiled. "Halfway is halfway, on every string."

Piper played the open E, then the octave at the twelfth, then both together. The two notes blended into one wide, ringing sound that filled the studio and hung in the air after she lifted her fingers away. She found her grandmother's note in her pocket, smoothed it out on the music stand, and wrote underneath it in pencil: "Found it. The twelfth fret is the middle." Then she played the pair again, louder this time.

story:
Natalie stood at the pharmacy counter waiting for her mom's allergy medicine, drumming her fingers on a display of copper bracelets. The sign above them said EASES ACHES AND PAINS, and beneath that, in smaller letters, a quote from a man named Dale: "After two weeks, my elbow pain was gone." Dale was holding up his wrist and grinning.

A woman with a shopping basket stopped beside Natalie and picked one up. "My brother swears by these," she said. "He wore one for his knee and says it cured him."

"Did anything else happen that month?" Natalie asked. "Like, did he rest it, or take something?"

The woman shrugged. "He probably did lots of things. He's retired, he golfs less in winter." She turned the bracelet over, checking the price.

Natalie had been arguing with her uncle Ray about this exact thing at Sunday dinner. He'd slapped his leather band on the table and said it fixed his back, and when she'd asked whether his new stretching routine might have helped instead, he'd said, "It worked for me, that's all I know." Her cousin Priya had leaned over and murmured, "That's called an anecdote," and later they'd looked it up: a story about one person's experience. The problem, the article said, was that a story like that couldn't show one thing caused another, because nobody had ruled out the other explanations. Knee pain gets better by itself sometimes. Elbows rest. Winters end.

"My dad's a mechanic," Natalie said to the woman. "He says you can't tell what fixed an engine if you changed three things at once. If you swapped the fuel filter and rebuilt a piston and then it ran, you don't know which one did it, or if it just dried out and started on its own." She picked up a box of the pharmacy's store-brand pain relievers instead. "This one has a little paper inside with studies, comparisons, how they tested it with lots of people, not just one guy like Dale."

The woman laughed and put the bracelet back. "One guy like Dale," she repeated. She squinted at the quote on the sign. "Though I suppose his pain was real to him. How it felt was subjective, even if the bracelet didn't cause it."

Natalie nodded. "The feeling can be true and the cure story can still be shaky." She felt her phone buzz: a text from Priya. Tell Uncle Ray we'll run the experiment. One month, bracelet on his left wrist only, stretches only in week two, diary every day.

Natalie grinned and typed back, "Deal. He has to sign it."

At the counter the pharmacist called her mom's name, and Natalie carried the white bag past the bracelet display, already drafting the first line of the diary in her head.

Anthony slid into the only empty desk, third row by the window, and listened to Ms. Ruiz assign science partners. A girl with a braid down her back turned around before the teacher even finished talking.

"I'm Priya," she said. "We got the decomposer project. Pill bugs, mushrooms, worms, any of those. I've been wanting a partner who actually cares, because last year my partner let me do everything."

"I care," Anthony said, though his mind was still on the moving truck that had left his old street three days ago. He thought about his friend Marcus, who had stood on the curb holding a folded map of the new town Anthony had drawn himself, useless now because Anthony had drawn the school in the wrong spot.

But his cousin Dev had also had a best friend once, and after Dev's family moved, the two of them just drifted, until a year later they had nothing to say. What was different about the friendships that survived moving? Anthony made a list on a napkin. The ones that lasted, like his uncle and his army buddy, called every single week. The ones that faded, like Dev's, nobody made the effort. It wasn't some mystery of fate. It was contact, regular contact, or nothing.

He called Marcus right then. It rang so long that Anthony almost hung up, sure this was all in vain.

"Yo," Marcus said. "I thought you forgot me already."

"Never. Look, I figured something out. Friends who move apart and stay close keep in touch regularly. Calls, messages, visits. The ones who don't, fade. So let's not be those guys."

"So what, we just text whenever?"

"No. Sunday, four o'clock, video call. Every week. Put it in your calendar."

"Every single week? For how long?"

"For as long as we want to still know each other," Anthony said.

There was a pause, and then Marcus laughed, the same laugh as always. "Okay. Sunday, four. I'm putting it in now. You better answer."

On Sunday Anthony set his phone against the salt shaker and waited, watching the screen, until the call chimed and Marcus's face filled it, holding up a slice of pizza from their old favorite place. "Wish you were here," Marcus said, "but this screen thing is going to have to do."

"Every Sunday," Anthony said. "Deal."

story:
Nolan had wanted a dog for three years, and today the wanting was finally over. His family had adopted a small brown puppy named Beans, and he was carrying her home down Juniper Street in the front pocket of his hoodie, her nose poking out like a joey riding in its mother's pouch. "You're not really a marsupial," he told her, "but you're close enough." Beans yawned at him. The houses along the street were tall and neat, the kind of affluent block where every lawn looked mowed by a ruler, and Nolan walked slowly so the walk would last.

Halfway home, Beans squirmed and whined, and Nolan realized she was chewing something. He tipped her gently out of the pocket and pried her jaw open. A shredded strip of minty wrapper stuck to her lip. His stomach dropped. He mentally ran through his backpack, the one he'd let her sniff at the shelter, the one that had sat open on his bed all morning. There had been gum in the front pocket. He remembered the silver packaging, and he remembered the words on it, sugar-free, because his mom bought that kind now. He dug through the backpack on the spot and counted seven empty wrappers where a full pack had been. She must have swallowed some while he was getting the leash.

He couldn't see inside Beans, so he worked from what he could see. She seemed fine, but that proved nothing, and he'd once read something on a poster at the dentist's office about sugar-free gum and dogs. He couldn't remember the details, only that it was bad, so he deduced the safest move: don't wait for symptoms, get to the vet now. He called his mom, and she turned the car around and met them at the corner.

The vet on Delmore Street took Beans straight back, and Nolan sat on a bench with his knees bouncing until the doctor came out. "Good timing," she said. "It was xylitol in that gum, the sweetener they use instead of sugar. Xylitol makes a dog's body release insulin, and insulin can drop her blood sugar to a dangerous level." She held up a syringe of sugar water. "We caught it early, so she'll be fine."

Nolan watched through the window as Beans, drowsy but awake, licked syrup from a small dish. He had wanted this dog for three years, and for three years he had imagined the fun parts, the fetch, the walks, the sleeping dog at his feet. He hadn't imagined checking backpacks, and he changed his mind right there on the bench about what owning a dog actually meant. It meant paying attention even when nothing looked wrong yet.

When they got home, Nolan emptied the backpack completely, gum and all, into a drawer high above Beans's best jump. He set the empty backpack on the floor and watched her climb inside anyway, tail wagging, her whole body disappearing except one brown ear. "Okay," he said, reaching in. "New rule. Nothing in the bag but you."

Julia stood at the chain-link fence at the edge of the playground, holding the new glasses in both hands like they might bite. Tomorrow was picture day, and if she wore them, they would be in the yearbook forever. If she didn't wear them, she would keep walking past her own friends without saying hi, which was what had happened twice this week alone.

Marcus found her there, bouncing a tennis ball against the blacktop. "You still hiding those? Put them on." He had been the one who figured out something was wrong with her eyes, back in October, when she kept copying his homework because she couldn't read the board.

"I don't want the whole school deciding they're weird." She shoved them into her pocket. "Besides, the eye doctor said I've got twenty forty vision. That's better than twenty twenty, right? Bigger number."

Marcus caught the ball and held it still. "My cousin had that. She said it's the other way around. It means you have to stand twenty feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight could read from forty."

"That makes no sense." But even as she said it, Julia thought about the eye chart, about how the big E at the top had been easy and every line under it had dissolved into gray smudges. She remembered squinting, leaning forward, the nurse telling her to stay behind the line on the floor. A normal person, standing twice as far back, would have read those same letters. The number wasn't a score. It was a distance.

"Fine," she said. "Test time." She walked to the far wall of the gym, where somebody had stenciled a small Wildcats logo by the door. "How far back do you think this is?"

"Like forty feet, maybe."

She pulled the glasses out and slid them on. The logo snapped into focus, every tooth in the bobcat's grin sharp and clean. She yanked them off, and it blurred back into a smear of purple. She put them on again. Off. On. It wasn't her imagination; the wall itself was changing, or rather, her eyes were. She thought of the arid blacktop in September, how she'd blamed the heat for the way everything shimmered.

Marcus threw her the ball from across the gym, and for the first time all season, she caught it without flinching, because she saw it the whole way in.

"So tomorrow," he said.

"Tomorrow, in the picture." She aimed the ball at the door and hit the bobcat square between the eyes.

Carter slid into his seat in the computer lab just as the bell finished ringing, which he counted as a personal victory. Mr. Reyes had assigned a project on internet safety, which meant a whole period of typing in a room that smelled like warm plastic and old sandwiches. He was halfway through a paragraph about strong passwords when the girl next to him, Priya, made a small choking noise.

"Look at this," she whispered, angling her screen toward him.

It was a screenshot. In it, a kid named Marcus, who everyone knew, had sent a private message to someone named Dylan saying their friend Kaya was "the most annoying person in the entire eighth grade, honestly." Now that screenshot was sitting in a different group chat, the big one with half the grade in it, with a row of shocked-face emojis underneath it.

"Wait," Carter said. "That was a private chat?"

"Dylan must have screenshotted it and shared it," Priya said. "Rough."

Carter stared at the image. He had always thought of private messages like passing a note in class, folded paper that only one person touched. But a screenshot, apparently, preserved the note forever, and the note went wherever the person who got it decided to take it. A private message was only as private as the people who read it. He tested the idea in his head: Marcus sent it to one person. One person showed forty. Yep. That tracked.

He looked at his own screen, where his draft to his friend Theo sat open in the corner. He had typed, "Mr. Reyes's tie today looks like a parrot lost a fight," and was about to hit send. His finger hovered. Theo was reliable. Theo had never leaked anything. But Dylan had probably seemed reliable too, right up until this morning.

Carter deleted the sentence and typed instead, "There is a bird. It is on a tie. That is all I will say publicly."

Theo, three rows over, turned around and mouthed, "Coward."

"You're welcome," Carter mouthed back.

Then something else occurred to him, and it was worse. He had sent Theo a private critique of Theo's book report last week, three whole paragraphs about the ending being "confusing in a way that felt accidental." If Theo ever got annoyed at him, that could end up in a group chat too. Carter opened the chat with Theo, found the message, and typed a follow-up: "Also I reread the ending and it's actually good, ignore all of that, especially the word accidental."

"Too late," Theo replied. "I already screenshotted it for the group."

Carter's stomach dropped for a full two seconds before the laughing emoji arrived.

"Kidding," Theo wrote. "But you should see your face from here."

"It's a very dignified face," Carter typed back, and then, after a moment, deleted that too.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
Sydney was halfway through a video about pad thai when every light in the house quit at once, and the fridge behind her dissolved into silence. She counted to ten in the dark, hoping the power would shrug itself back on, then felt her way to the junk drawer and dug out the emergency candles Grandma insisted on keeping there. Soon the living room flickered with four small flames, and Sydney flopped onto the couch beside her grandfather, who was already grinning like the darkness was a treat.

"Good evening for stories," he said. He leaned toward the candlelight. "Back in 2003, I was working in an office when the power went out, and I had to walk all the way home. It was the Northeast blackout, August 14, 2003, and it cut power to about 55 million people. Whole parts of the northeastern United States, plus Ontario, in Canada, all dark at once."

Sydney sat up. "Fifty-five million? How do you even know it was that many?"

"That's what everyone said afterward. Streets full of people walking home, strangers sharing water bottles, restaurants giving away melting ice cream." He laughed. "Best free cuisine I ever had, let me tell you."

Sydney's phone buzzed with one last text before it died, from her friend Marisol down the block: "Look out your front window!!" Sydney carried a candle to the window, careful not to drip wax on the sill. Every streetlight she could see was dark. Every porch light, every glowing window, gone. But then she noticed something odd. Far off, past the park, the sky had a faint orange shimmer of city light, way over on the east side.

She hurried back to the couch, thinking hard. If the whole grid were down like in her grandfather's story, everything would be black in every direction. But the east side still glowed. That meant the outage had edges, which meant it had a boundary somewhere, and boundaries meant the problem was local, not enormous. She tested the idea out loud. "Grandpa, it's not fifty-five million people this time. I think it's just us, this neighborhood. Maybe one little section."

He raised his eyebrows. "How do you figure?"

"Because I can see lights over east. Fifty-five million people would include them, probably."

Just then a knock rattled the door, and there stood Marisol with a flashlight and a printed flyer from the utility crew on her corner: scheduled maintenance, power back by nine, sorry for the inconvenience. Sydney snatched it and read it by candle flame.

"Nine o'clock!" she shouted. "Grandpa, we have two whole hours. Tell me the ice cream part again."

story:
The paper plate sagged under David's slice of cake as he slid onto the porch bench beside his grandmother, who was holding up an empty mug like a trophy. "Two days ago I had the worst headache of my life," she announced to the whole reunion. "Worse than any in years. Then I drank that new ginger tea my neighbor brought over, and by evening it was gone. I'm telling you, that tea is a miracle." Aunt Rosa immediately asked for the brand name, and Uncle Marcus said he'd order a case. David took a bite of cake and wondered something he couldn't quite let go of: would the headache have eased anyway, even if she'd drunk nothing but tap water?

He couldn't test a headache, but he could test a chart. His grandmother kept a little calendar in her purse, and she let him look at it because she loved showing off her careful penmanship. On it she rated every headache from one to ten, and he copied three months of ratings onto graph paper that evening, using a pencil from his backpack. His cousin Marcus Jr., twelve like him, leaned over his shoulder. Marcus Jr. wanted to be a sports announcer and narrated everything, including this. "David versus the mystery of the tea," he intoned. "The crowd is on its feet."

David drew a dot for each headache, then ran his pencil along a diagonal line from the low ratings in the corner to the high ones. The pattern jumped out at him. The tens, the worst headaches, were almost always followed by fours or fives. The bad days fell back toward the ordinary ones, over and over, like coins dropped from a table always landing somewhere near the floor. He sat back. So the tea hadn't necessarily done anything. When Grandma felt her worst, the next day was bound to be more normal no matter what she drank. His quiet assumption that the tea must have caused the cure suddenly looked shaky.

But there was a twist he hadn't expected. "What did you take for the headaches before the tea?" he asked her. She squinted at the calendar. "Whatever your grandfather handed me. Aspirin, usually." David checked the dates. The aspirin days showed the same slide from bad to ordinary. So the pattern swallowed both remedies. "There's a name for this," he said slowly, remembering a phrase from a library book he'd skimmed. "Regression to the mean. It's called regression to the mean." Marcus Jr. cupped his hands around his mouth. "In a stunning upset, the tea loses to nothing at all!"

Grandma sniffed and lifted her mug again, and the steam rising from the fresh tea seemed to symbolize her stubbornness better than any words could. "You can keep your diagonal line," she said. "The tea stays." She took a long, deliberate sip, and winked at him over the rim.
