activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Kayla had the best seat in the living room, the corner of the couch where she could see the TV and the door to the kitchen at the same time, and she was wrapped in the striped blanket she used to insulate herself against the draft that seeped under the window every winter. Her uncle had claimed that spot for years, but tonight he was stuck in the folding chair, because Kayla had gotten to the couch first and he had let her keep it. She still remembered that. Last spring, when her team had lost the semifinal, he had given up the seat to a neighbor kid and the team had lost anyway, and ever since he had a theory that seat assignments mattered.

The Wolverines were up by four with six minutes left. Down the block in their affluent neighborhood, half the houses probably had the same game on, and every so often a muffled cheer rolled through the walls like the houses themselves were shouting.

"That's it, they've got it," her cousin Marcus said, bouncing a throw pillow off his knee. "They're unstoppable."

Kayla wasn't so sure. The Wolverines had been shaky all season, and something kept nagging at her. She grabbed her tablet and pulled up the standings, scrolling through game after game. Home games were marked with a little house symbol, and away games with a plane. She started counting.

"What are you doing?" Marcus leaned over, chewing a pretzel.

"Counting. Look." She turned the screen toward him. "At home they've won way more than they've lost. On the road it's the opposite." She had tallied it across a whole page, and the pattern held even though road games and home games were the same sport, the same players, the same rules. Something invisible was tilting things.

"So?"

"So that's why they win here. It's a real thing, it's called home advantage," she said. "In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games."

Marcus shook his head. "That's not why. They won because Coach Bell switched to the press in the third quarter."

"Then explain the pattern." Kayla tapped the tally marks. "If it's just the press, why does it only work at home?"

Marcus opened his mouth, then closed it, then pointed at the screen, where the other team had just cut the lead to two. "Because... watch the game, that's why."

Uncle Ray laughed from the folding chair. "My official diagnosis is that neither of you can enjoy anything." But he was grinning, and he craned his neck to look at Kayla's tally marks, and he didn't argue with them either.

Kayla thought about last spring again, the semifinal loss, how she had blamed the referee for weeks. Maybe the truth was smaller and stranger than that. Maybe there were forces you couldn't see on the court, tilting games one direction, and you could only catch them by counting.

The Wolverines missed a free throw. Marcus groaned and buried his face in the pillow. With two minutes left, Kayla pulled the blanket tighter, set the tablet on her lap, tally side up, and said, "Count with me. If they pull this out, it fits."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
story:
Antoine sat at the kitchen computer with a bag of chips and a grudge. His cousin Marcus had commented on the town history page: "Everyone says Riverside was founded in 1871, but my grandpa swears it was 1879. That's just his opinion against yours." Antoine typed back, "No, it's a claim. Somebody's right and somebody's wrong." Then he stared at the screen, because he had no idea how to prove it.

He started with the obvious and set the search to exclude anything written after 1950, which wiped out a hundred tourist sites that all copied each other. What was left was a link to the county library's old newspaper archive, scanned page by page. Mom wandered past with her prescription bag from the pharmacy and said dinner was in an hour. "One thing first," Antoine said, and clicked.

The archive was slow and fussy, and half the pages were just smudges. He tried "1871" and got nothing but grain prices. He tried "founding" and got a flood. There it was, a front page from June 1871 with a photograph of men in dark coats standing around a rough wooden sign that said RIVERSIDE. Beside it ran a letter from the land agent, who wrote that the first lots would be sold in July, and a column of official figures from the county recorder listing the lots and their buyers.

Antoine's heart was going fast. On a video call, Marcus squinted at the scanned page Antoine held up to his webcam. "What am I looking at?"

"A primary source," Antoine said. "A firsthand record from the time itself. The letter, the photograph, the official data. It's the best place to check a claim." He scrolled so Marcus could read the land agent's words himself. "Somebody in 1871 wrote this while it was happening. They couldn't have known we'd be arguing about it."

Marcus was quiet for a second. "Okay. So Grandpa's 1879 thing is wrong." He rubbed his chin. "Unless that's when the town got its charter or something." Antoine pulled up a later page and found it: the incorporation paperwork filed eight years after the founding, in 1879. "You were both a little right," Antoine said. "Your grandpa was remembering the charter year, not the founding." Marcus laughed, and Antoine laughed too, the grudge gone.

They stayed on the call planning a project for the heritage fair, a printed copy of that 1871 front page with a note pinned beside it about the 1879 charter. Antoine bookmarked the archive, then printed the page on the good paper, not the flimsy stuff, because his dad had warned him the cheap sheets were flammable near the space heater. He carried the warm page to his room and taped it above his desk, the men in dark coats still staring out of 1871, waiting for everyone else to catch up.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
On the first morning of Grandma's visit, Lea sat on the end of the guest bed while Grandma unpacked her suitcase, and they talked about everything: the flight, the neighbors' new dog, Lea's science project. Grandma answered every question right away, laughing at all the right moments. Lea decided the week was going to be perfect.

The trouble started on Wednesday at the train station. Lea and Grandma were meeting Aunt Rosa, and the station roared with announcements, rolling suitcases, and a man playing saxophone near the ticket machines. Lea said, "Aunt Rosa's train comes at noon, right?" Grandma frowned and said, "Tulips? In June?" Lea tried again, slower, and Grandma guessed "new shoes." After the third try, Grandma just smiled and nodded at whatever Lea said, and Lea felt her stomach drop. At home that same question would have gotten an instant answer.

Lea started testing. In the quiet of the kitchen, she asked Grandma ordinary questions and Grandma caught every word, even when Lea mumbled. In the noisy cafeteria at school, when Grandma came for Grandparents' Day, the same questions fell apart, and Grandma kept leaning in and guessing wrong. Lea wrote her results in her notebook like a scientist. Quiet meant yes. Noise meant no. It wasn't that Grandma couldn't hear, because she heard fine when the room was silent. It was the noise that stole the words away. Her science teacher had once said the class shouldn't be biased toward one experiment, so Lea tried a different place, the loud coffee shop, and got the same result. The pattern held.

That night Lea left a note on the guest bed before Grandma went to sleep. "Dear Grandma," she wrote, "I noticed you can hear me great in the kitchen but the train station was a disaster. I don't think your ears are the problem. I think the background noise is. Want to help me test it tomorrow? We can sit in the park away from the crowd. Love, Lea." In the morning Grandma waved the note at her over breakfast. "So that's why I've been nodding like a fool in restaurants," she said. "My sister figured this out years ago and I never believed her."

They became a team after that. When the family went to the Saturday farmers market, Lea steered Grandma to the quiet end by the flower stall before asking whether they should buy peaches or plums. When Aunt Rosa wanted Grandma to participate in the trivia night at the community center, Lea asked the organizer if their table could be moved away from the speakers, and their team came in second. Grandma's pivot from "I'll just stay home where it's quiet" to "find me a corner seat and I'm in" happened somewhere around Thursday, and Lea knew exactly why.

On the last night of the visit, they sat together on the guest bed with the door shut and the house still. "You solved it," Grandma said. "Nobody ever told me it was the noise. They just kept saying I was going deaf." Lea grinned and flipped to the back of her notebook, where she had drawn a chart with two columns, Quiet and Noisy, full of checkmarks and X's. "Science," she said, and held it up for Grandma to see.
